headline: Comer: stopgap funding bill is hemp's best shot before 11 December
dek: Rep. James Comer told Kentucky hemp firms no stand-alone bill will get a vote before 11 December, leaving a must-pass funding bill as the last route.
key_points: Rep. James Comer (R-KY) told Kentucky hemp businesses this week he does not expect a stand-alone hemp bill to get a vote before the 11 December deadline.
He said the best chance is to attach hemp language to the next continuing resolution, the same kind of stopgap funding bill that created the ban in November 2025.
Federal funding also runs out on 11 December, so the hemp deadline and the shutdown deadline now fall on the same day.
At least four bills to delay or repeal the new hemp definition are pending; none has moved out of committee.
body: The fight over the federal hemp THC ban now comes down to one bill that has not been written yet. Rep. James Comer, the Kentucky Republican who chairs the House Oversight Committee, told Kentucky hemp industry members this week that he does not expect any stand-alone hemp bill to get a floor vote before 11 December, when most of the new federal hemp definition takes effect, Spectrum News reported on 13 November.

Instead, Comer said the industry's best hope is to ride on legislation that cannot fail. In his view the only bill that truly has to pass is another continuing resolution, the stopgap that keeps the government funded. His goal, he said, is to get hemp protections onto "a bill that is going to pass." As of this morning, 16 November, that leaves 25 days.
## Why the spending bill matters

The ban itself came from a spending bill. The FY2026 agriculture appropriations act, enacted on 12 November 2025 as Public Law 119-37 at the end of that autumn's shutdown, rewrote the federal definition of hemp, according to the Congressional Research Service summary on Congress.gov. It moved the THC test from delta-9 THC alone to total THC and excluded many hemp-derived cannabinoid products, including finished products with more than 0.4 milligrams of total THC per container, The Marijuana Herald reported.

That cap would cover most hemp THC drinks and gummies on the market today, and many full-spectrum CBD products that carry trace THC. Congress then pushed most of the change back by a month in a continuing resolution signed on 2 September, moving the date from 12 November to 11 December. The part covering cannabinoids that the plant cannot produce naturally was left out of that delay and took effect on 12 November, as we reported that day.

The 11 December date is also when current government funding expires. That puts the hemp deadline and the next funding deadline on the same calendar square, and it is why Comer sees the next stopgap as the vehicle.
> The hemp ban was born in a funding bill, and on 11 December it lives or dies in the next one.
## A plan Comer has tried before

This is not a new strategy for Comer. In January he told Roll Call he was working with House leadership to put a delay into the funding bill due at the end of that month, and he co-sponsored a bill from Rep. Jim Baird (R-IN) that would push the effective date to November 2028. That push did not produce a delay at the time; the only reprieve so far came in the 2 September stopgap, and it bought one month.

Comer has also said hemp needs rules rather than a ban. In January he told Roll Call the industry should not be regulated like a drug or a supplement, but that some type of regulatory framework is needed. This week his message to Kentucky growers was more personal: he said he has farmer friends planning to grow hemp next year and labs that have made large investments, and that the industry is working.
## Bills on the shelf

Several bills already sit in Congress. H.R. 7024, H.R. 7010 and S. 3686 would give the industry more time, and H.R. 6209 would repeal the changes to the hemp definition outright, according to The Marijuana Herald. H.R. 6209, the American Hemp Protection Act from Rep. Nancy Mace (R-SC), was introduced on 20 November 2025 and was referred to a House Agriculture subcommittee on 13 January, where it has stayed, Congress.gov shows.

Outside Congress, the National Hemp Association says it and a coalition of more than 70 organisations are pushing a short-term bridge, the American Hemp Certainty Act, before the deadline, and a fuller framework called the Goodness of Hemp Act for the next Congress.

The Senate is split on the question. As we reported on 14 November, Sen. Pete Ricketts (R-NE) wants no further delay, while Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D-MN) says she is working on a bipartisan fix. Democrats take control of Congress in January, but that is after the deadline: any change before 11 December has to pass the current Congress.
## What businesses are doing now

Kentucky retailers are already counting down. Dee Dee Taylor, who owns 502 Hemp in Louisville and leads the Kentucky Hemp Association, told Spectrum News her whole business could become illegal on the deadline, which carries no grace period for unsold inventory or processed material. She said she would accept new taxes on hemp products if that kept stores open.

States are not waiting either. Maryland's Cannabis Administration told dispensaries on 13 November that from 11 December, hemp products that no longer meet the federal definition can only be sold from the restricted service area, and only if they meet cannabis manufacturing, testing, packaging and labelling rules, IgniteIt reported. Charlotte's Web said in its quarterly filing that some of its full-spectrum CBD products would no longer meet the federal definition if the change takes effect as scheduled.
## What it means

For hemp brands, distributors and retailers, the realistic plan is now two plans: one for a last-minute rider in a stopgap, and one for a ban that arrives on schedule. Riders are often traded away in end-of-year funding talks, and short stopgaps tend to carry little policy language. A rider would also need the support of House and Senate leaders and the White House, not only hemp-state members.

For licensed cannabis operators the outcome matters too. A ban would push intoxicating hemp products out of gas stations and smoke shops, and in states like Maryland into dispensaries. A rider that sets rules instead could keep a parallel market alive.
## What to watch

Watch for the text of the next continuing resolution, likely in the first days of December, and whether it carries any hemp language. Watch statements from House and Senate appropriations leaders, and from Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-KY), who championed the original change. In Illinois, a federal judge hears a challenge to the state's own hemp limits on 19 November.
